§ 1155-8 ] [Ch .36 .CRIMES AND PUNISHMENTS .
Felonies - Rape , Abduction .
§ 1155. Carnally knowing female under sixteen, or an idiot. Whoever shall car-
nally know a female under the age of sixteen years , or an idiot , shall
be confined in the penitentiary not less than ten nor more than twenty
years . ( Section as amended by act March 16 , 1906. )
§ 1156. Abduction of girlunder fourteen. Whoever , being above the age of
fourteen years , shall unlawfully take , without her consent , any unmarried
girl , under the age of fourteen years , out of the possession of her father ,
mother , or other person having the lawful custody and charge of her .
against the will and consent of such person , shall be confined in the
penitentiary from one to two years , or fined from one to five hundred dol-
lars , or both , at the discretion of the jury .
§ 1157. Decoying or enticing away or harboring child under ten. Whoever , being
above the age of fourteen years , shall unlawfully lead or take away , or
decoy , or entice away , or detain any child under the age of ten years , with
intent to deprive the parent or other person having the lawful care,
charge or possession of such child , or with intent to steal any article of
value upon or about the person of such child , or shall , with any such
intention , receive , conceal or harbor such child , knowing it to have been
so taken or enticed away , shall be confined in the penitentiary not less
than one nor more than three years . But no person claiming in good
faith to be the parent of such child , or to have the right to its possession ,
shall incur the penalty prescribed in this or the next preceding section .
§ 1157a . Holding person for ransom - jurisdiction. If any person or persons
shall , forcibly or otherwise , hold any person against their will for the
purpose of unlawfully obtaining a ransom for the release of said person
or aid or abet any person thus offending , shall , on conviction thereof ,be
deemed guilty of a felony , and shall be confined in the penitentiary not
less than two nor more than twenty -one years . Any person or persons
charged with such offense may be tried in any county into or through
which the person or child so seized , inveigled , decoyed , kidnapped ,
abducted or otherwise taken shall have been carried or brought . (This
section is an act of March 21 , 1902. )
§ 1158. Unlawfully taking or detaining woman against her will. Whoever shall
unlawfully take or detain any woman against her will , with intent to
marry such woman , or have her married to another , or with intent to
have carnal knowledge with her himself , or that another shall have such
knowledge , shall be confined in the penitentiary not less than two nor
more than seven years .
§ 1158. (1) Constituents of offense. It is
sufficientif the act was done without the
consent of the woman ; and if she was un-
conscious, or incapable of exercisingher will,
the act should be regarded as done without
her consent. Malone v . Com ., 91 Ky ., 307 ;
12 R., 895 ; 15 S. W. , 856 ; Couch v. Com ., 16
R., 477 ; 29 S. W. ,29.
(2) Degree of offense. The statute creates
a lesseroffensethan that of rape or attempt
to commit rape. Evans v . Com ., 79 Ky ., 414 ;
3 R., 30 ; Howell v. Com ., 5 R., 174. And
under an indictment for rape the accused
may be convicted of unlawfully detaining a
woman . Fagan v. Com ., 18 R., 714; 38 S.W.,
431.
(3) Indictment charging accused with un-

§ 1322. **Sunday—barbering on.** That any person who engages in the business of barbering on Sunday shall be deemed guilty of a misdemeanor, and, upon conviction thereof, shall be fined not more than five dollars, and upon a second conviction for a like offense, shall be fined not less than ten dollars and not more than twenty-five dollars, or imprisoned in the county jail for a period of not less than five days nor more than ten days, or be both fined and imprisoned, at the discretion of the court. (*Section is act of March 27, 1893.*)

§ 1323. **Sunday—hunting on.** If any person shall hunt game, with a gun or dogs, on the Sabbath, he shall be fined not less than five nor more than fifty dollars for each offense.

§ 1324. **Driving unbranded sheep on highway.** If any person shall drive sheep for a distance of more than ten miles along a public road, without each sheep being plainly branded, or marked with one or more letters or crosses, he shall be fined not less than two nor more than ten dollars for each sheep so driven.

§ 1325. **Furnishing false pedigree of stock.** Any person who shall knowingly and willfully furnish to any purchaser of stock any false pedigree of such stock, shall, upon conviction thereof, be fined in any sum not less than one hundred nor more than one thousand dollars, or imprisoned in the county jail not less than three nor more than twelve months, or both so fined and imprisoned.

None of these sections mention race, nor do they contain any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. The regulations pertain to animal husbandry, public safety on roads, and fair practices in horse racing. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

§ 1334. Person dying on boat - duty of master . If any person shall die on
board of a steamer or other water -craft , within this State , if not claimed
by a friend , the master or other officer in command shall cause the dead
body to be buried on shore , at least four feet deep . Such master or other
officer failing so to do shall be fined not less than two hundred dollars ,
and the vessel shall be liable for the payment of it.
§ 1335. Disinterring buried bodies. Whoever shall unlawfully or secretly
disinter or displace any dead human body from the grave or vault in
which it has been deposited , shall be fined not less than two hundred nor
more than one thousand dollars , and imprisoned not less than two nor
more than six months .
§ 1336. Mutilation of graves and tombs in cemetery . Any person who shall
willfully mutilate the graves , monuments , fences , shrubbery , ornaments ,
grounds or buildings in or inclosing any cemetery or place of sepulture ;
or shall violate the grave of any person by willfully destroying , remov-
ing or injuring the head or foot stone , or the tomb over , or the inclosure
protecting , any grave , or by digging into , or plowing over or removing
any ornament , shrubbery or flower placed upon any grave or lot , shall be
fined not less than ten nor than one hundred dollars , or imprisoned
not exceeding six months , or both , as the jury may determine .
§ 1337. Superintendent of cemetery — duties— penalties. The superintendent of
any incorporated cemetery or grave -yard shall be removed for the viola-
tion of any of the provisions of the charters of such cemeteries or grave-
yards , and shall also be fined not less than ten nor more than one hun-
dred dollars . (Sce , further , sec . 207. )

tence of imprisonment , or to be whipped , or under a capias , escapes jail ,
or if a person lawfully arrested upon a charge for a violation of the crim-

or guard , he shall be confined in jail not less than six nor more than
twelve months . (Penalty for aiding escape , see secs . 1235 , 1239 , 1357. )

classification.summary: This statute makes it a misdemeanor for any person to willfully entice, persuade, or otherwise influence a laborer who has contracted for a fixed period to abandon their contract before its expiration without the employer's consent. The offender would be fined and liable for damages to the injured party.
classification.reasoning: The statute addresses the issue of laborers breaking contracts. While labor laws can sometimes have racial implications, this particular statute does not contain any explicit or implicit racial indicators. It applies to any laborer and any employer without distinction of race. Therefore, it is not classified as a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: DESCENT AND DISTRIBUTION
classification.summary: This statute addresses the legitimacy and inheritance rights of children born from slave marriages. It states that children born from cohabitation between enslaved individuals as husband and wife are considered lawful children and legal heirs. However, if either parent later legally marries another person and has children from that subsequent marriage, the children from the slave marriage will only inherit a proportion of the property based on the ratio of children from the slave marriage to children from the subsequent legal marriage. The act also specifies that it does not apply if the property has already been sold to innocent purchasers or divided.
classification.reasoning: The statute explicitly mentions 'colored persons' and 'slave marriages,' directly indicating a racial component. While it aims to legitimize children of slave marriages, the provision for proportional inheritance based on subsequent legal marriages introduces a discriminatory element that reflects the social and legal structures of the Jim Crow era, particularly concerning the recognition and rights of formerly enslaved individuals and their descendants. The document type is 'codes' as it appears to be part of a compiled statute collection (Kentucky Statutes 1909).

entries.reviewer_note:
The specification that "That this act
shall not apply in any case where the property of either father or mother
has passed to innocent purchasers or heretofor édivided out or sold, or
estate through her" indicates that if a white person had acquired the parents' property, the Black child would be essentially cut off from gaining it, regardless of the desire of the late parent(s).

classification.title: Descent and Distribution
classification.summary: This statute outlines the property and monetary allowances that are to be set aside for a widow and/or infant children from a deceased husband's estate. It details specific items such as household goods, tools, and provisions, with maximum monetary values for each. It also addresses situations where these items are not on hand and provides for alternative property or money. The statute specifies procedures for appraisers and the conditions under which a widow can renounce a will to claim her dower and distributable share.
classification.reasoning: The statute deals with inheritance and the rights of a widow and children to a portion of the deceased husband's estate. It specifies allowances for household goods, tools, and provisions. There is no mention of race, and the provisions appear to apply universally to all widows and children regardless of race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it appears to be part of a compiled set of statutes from 1909.

classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1909 outlines rules for inheritance and distribution of estates. Specifically, it details conditions under which a wife or husband living in adultery forfeits their right to inherit personalty from their deceased spouse, with exceptions for reconciliation. It also defines advancements (gifts of property or money) made by parents or grandparents to descendants and how these are accounted for in the distribution of the remaining estate to ensure proportionate equality among heirs.

There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. The language used is neutral and applies to all individuals regardless of their racial background. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This statute clarifies that advancements made to distributees (heirs) do not affect the distributable share of the widow in the deceased's personal estate. classification.reasoning: The provided statute text discusses the legal concept of 'advancements' in the context of inheritance and estate distribution. It details how gifts or money given to heirs during the lifetime of the deceased are accounted for when settling the estate. There is no mention of race, nor any indication of differential treatment based on race. The statute appears to be a general civil law concerning property and inheritance. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

The statute also references previous acts and judicial interpretations related to timber assessment.

It establishes fees for salvaging, a lien for those fees, and a process for selling unclaimed property. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial discrimination. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it is presented as part of a compiled statute (Kentucky Statutes 1909).

The statute further states that soldiers, seamen, and marines of the U.S. military are not considered residents and cannot vote. It also addresses municipal elections requiring poll-tax payment and defines election officers. Additionally, it details the division of election precincts based on voter numbers and the process for changing voting places.

The statute specifies that certain emblems, such as the national flag or state seal, cannot be used as devices on ballots.

It does not contain any language that explicitly or implicitly discriminates based on race. The provisions are procedural and apply to all candidates and political parties. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

§ 1457. Secretary of State to certify to county clerks names of candidates- vacancy
in General Assembly . Not less than twenty days before the election of such
officers as are required to file their certificate of nomination with the
Secretary of State said Secretary of State shall certify to the respective
county court clerks of the various counties which are entitled under the
law to participate in the election of the respective candidates , the name
and place of residence of each candidate for each respective office, as
specified in the certificates and petitions of nomination filed with him ,
and shall designate therein , subject to the provisions of this act , the
device under which the group or list of candidates , or candidate , of each
party shall be printed , in the order in which they shall be arranged on
the ballot : Provided , however , Should a vacancy occur in the General
Assembly and a writ of election issued to fill said vacancy , the petition
or certificate of nomination may be filed ten days before the day of elec-
tion , and if filed with the Secretary of State shall be immediately certi-
fied to the proper county court clerks . No writ for the election of a mem
ber of the General Assembly shall be issued , except so as to enable the
sheriff to give notice thereof , as now provided by law , at least fifteen days
before the day of election . (This section is sec . 2 of an act of October
16 , 1900 , and , as it covers every part of the original section , it is inserted
as a substitute for it.)
§ 1457a . Penalty against county clerk for failingto print ballots correctly. If the
county court clerk shall willfully and knowingly refuse or fail to have
the name of any candidate printed upon the official ballot in the manner
provided for in this act he shall forfeit his office and be guilty of a
felony , and , upon conviction , be confined in the penitentiary for not less
than one year nor more than three years . (This section is sec . 3 of an
act of October 16 , 1900. )
§ 1458. Names certified when not to be printed on ballots. The Secretary of
State shall not certify the name of a candidate whose certificate of nomi-
nation shall have been filed in his office who shall have notified him in
writing , signed and executed with the formalities prescribed for the
execution of an instrument to entitle it to record , that he will not accept
the nomination contained in the certificate or petition of nomination .
The county clerk shall not cause to be published on the regular ballots,
according to section 1460 hereof , the name of any candidate whose certifi-
cate or petition of nomination shall have been filed in his office who shall
have notified him in like manner that he will not accept the nomination .
The names of such candidates shall not be included in the names of the
candidates to be printed in the ballots as hereinafter provided .

§ 1467. Voting places- booths duties of sheriff. It shall be the duty of the
sheriff in each county , before each election , to secure in each precinct of
the county a suitable room in which to hold the election , and to have
placed therein sufficient number of booths or compartments in which
electors shall mark their ballots , screened from observation . The number
of such booths shall not be less than one to every one hundred voters , and
one for every fraction of one hundred voters exceeding fifty who voted
at the last preceding election in such precinct . Each booth shall have
three sides inclosed , one side in front to open and shut by a door , swing-
ing outward , or to be closed with a curtain ; and each booth shall be
about six feet high and about three feet square , and shall contain a shelf
at least one foot wide at a convenient height for writing , and the door
or curtain shall extend to within two feet of the floor , which shall be
closed while the voter is preparing his ballot , and such booths shall be
well lighted . Booths shall be so arranged that all the officers of election
can see whether more than one voter enters any of such booths at one
time ; and the sheriff of election , in each precinct , shall have the care and
custody of said booths , and may direct in whose custody they shall re-
main after an election . No person , other than the election officers and
the challengers allowed by law , and those admitted for the purpose of
voting , as hereinafter provided , shall be permitted within said room while
the vote is being polled , except by authority of the election officers to
keep order and enforce the law . The expense of rooms and booths shall
be paid in the same manner as other election expenses .
§ 1468. Ballot boxes - character of duties of sheriff. It shall be the duty of
the sheriff of each county , or the officer acting for him when , for any
cause , the sheriff can not act , to provide for each precinct or voting place
in the county , and at the expense of the county , to be paid out of the
county funds upon order of the county court and allowed by the fiscal
court , a strong and well -made ballot box , sufficiently large to contain all
the ballots to be cast at the precinct or voting place to which it is sent ;
such box to have on it a lid , working on hinges , and provided with two
locks of different kinds and combinations , so that the key of the one will
not unlock the other . An aperture , sufficient only for the insertion of a
single ballot , shall be made in each box . Such box shall , not less than
three days before the day for holding an election , be , by the sheriff or
other officer acting for him , delivered to the officers of the election in each
precinct or voting place . The officers of the election , before the voting
begins , shall see that no ballots are in the box , and shall thereupon

4. Oath of election officers—when voters may select. Should the County Board of Election Commissioners fail to appoint such officers of election, or if any of such officers fail to attend for thirty minutes after the time for commencing the election, or refuse to act, the officer in attendance representing the same political party of the absentee shall appoint a suitable person to act in his stead for that election; or if both representatives of the same political party are absent, qualified voters present affiliating with the party of said two absentees shall elect, *viva voce*, suitable persons to act in their stead. Each officer of election shall, before entering upon the duties of his office, take an oath faithfully to discharge his duties as such officer before some person authorized to administer an oath, or if no such officer be present it may be administered by the clerk of the election, who shall in turn be sworn by one of the judges of election.

5. County board to canvass returns—when and where to meet—certificates of election—poll-books and ballots. Said County Board of Election Commissioners shall constitute a board for examining and canvassing the election returns of each county and awarding and issuing certificates of election. Any two of the members of said board may constitute the board, but if either be a candidate he shall have no voice in the decision of his own case. If from any cause two of the members of the board can not act, in whole or in part, in examining and canvassing the returns their places shall be supplied as in case of vacancies in such board. Within two days next after an election the sheriff shall deposit with the clerk of the county court the returns from the different precincts. classification.summary: This statute outlines the homestead exemption in Kentucky, protecting a certain amount of land and dwelling from sale under execution, attachment, or judgment for debts incurred after June 1, 1866. It specifies conditions for the exemption, such as the debtor being an actual bona fide housekeeper with a family, and exceptions for mortgages, purchase money, and debts existing prior to land purchase or improvements. The statute also details conditions for abandonment of the homestead right and its re-establishment, as well as its applicability to inherited property and its disposition by will. It also notes that the homestead exemption generally does not apply to debts due the State, with some exceptions.

classification.title: Fees Allowed to Jailers and Magistrates
classification.summary: This statute outlines the fees that jailers and magistrates are allowed to charge for various services. For jailers, these include attending courts, furnishing fuel and light, putting prisoners in irons, and keeping and dieting prisoners. The statute specifies that fees for keeping and dieting prisoners are to be paid by the county levy, unless the prisoner is confined for a breach of city/town by-laws or ordinances, or for violation of a statute where the city/town benefits from the fine, in which case the city/town pays. Fees for imprisoning and releasing misdemeanor offenders are also paid by the county levy, with the same exception for city/town fines. Felony offenders' imprisonment and release fees are paid by the State Treasury. For magistrates, fees are listed for issuing warrants, summons, subpoenas, and attachments.
classification.reasoning: The statute details the fees for jailers and magistrates. While it mentions different payment sources (county levy, city/town, state treasury) based on the offense and the beneficiary of the fine, it does not contain any explicit or implicit racial classifications or distinctions. The fees and services described are general and apply to all individuals regardless of race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the process for fiscal courts to issue bonds for building bridges. It details the role of a commissioner in selling these bonds, the levying of an ad valorem tax to pay interest and redeem the bonds (with a limit of fifty cents per one hundred dollars worth of property), the collection of this tax by the sheriff, and the requirement for the sheriff to execute a bond for faithful performance. It also specifies that the question of issuing bonds must be submitted to a vote of legal voters, with notice requirements for the election.
classification.reasoning: The statute concerns the financing and construction of bridges through the issuance of bonds and the levying of taxes. It outlines the procedural steps for fiscal courts, commissioners, and sheriffs in this process. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial segregation or discrimination. The voting aspect refers to 'all legal voters of the county,' which, in the context of the time, would have included all eligible voters regardless of race, though the actual exercise of that right for Black citizens was often suppressed by other means not present in this specific statute. Therefore, this statute is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: County Levy - Collection of
classification.summary: This statute outlines the authority of fiscal courts in Kentucky counties to levy and collect poll and ad valorem taxes. These taxes are designated for paying existing indebtedness, defraying current and necessary county expenses, or for the maintenance of public roads. The statute specifies limits on the poll tax ($1.50 per male person 21 or older) and the ad valorem tax (50 cents per $100 of taxable property). It also details the process for tax collection, including the requirement for collectors (sheriffs) to execute bonds, their compensation, and annual settlements. The statute explicitly states that taxes cannot be levied to pay railroad bonded indebtedness or interest on such debt.
classification.reasoning: The statute deals with the fiscal management of counties, specifically the levying and collection of taxes for general county purposes and road maintenance. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial discrimination. The tax structure and collection mechanisms described are applied generally to all residents and property within the county. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

It outlines various scenarios where such conveyances are considered voidable, including transfers to creditors or colluding strangers, and specifies conditions under which bona fide purchasers and creditors are protected. The statute also details conditions under which preferred creditors must refund money, the effect of prior agreements on assignments, requirements for recording mortgages, and how simultaneous and pre-existing debts are treated in such conveyances. It also addresses actions by sureties and voluntary assignments.

classification.title: Fruit Trees Diseased
classification.summary: This statute makes it unlawful to knowingly keep plum, cherry, or other trees infected with the 'black knot' disease. Such infected trees are declared public nuisances, and no damages will be awarded for entering premises to cut away or destroy infected parts or trees. County judges are authorized to appoint three freeholder fruit-growers as commissioners to address the disease if it exists or is apprehended. The commissioners must file acceptances, and the county clerk will serve as their clerk, keeping records of their proceedings.
classification.reasoning: The statute addresses the control of a plant disease ('black knot') affecting fruit trees. It outlines procedures for identifying and removing infected trees and the appointment of commissioners to manage the issue. There is no mention of race, and the subject matter is purely agricultural and public health related to plants. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: Geological Department - Officials not to speculate in mineral lands or make private reports.
classification.summary: This statute outlines regulations for employees and officials of the Geological Survey. It prohibits them from speculating in mineral lands, engaging in the buying or selling of such lands, or providing private information about discoveries. They are permitted to share information with the actual landowner and can publish important findings in public journals or scientific societies with approval. They may also conduct examinations for mineral property owners for development purposes, provided it doesn't impede the survey's progress. Violations can lead to removal from the survey.

classification.title: GUARDIANS, BOARD OF FOR CHILDREN IN CERTAIN COUNTIES
classification.summary: This statute establishes a Board of Children's Guardians in counties with cities of the first class. The board is composed of six persons, two of whom shall be colored. The board has the care and supervision of neglected and dependent children under sixteen years of age and can commit them to various institutions or have them indentured or adopted. The explicit mention of 'two of whom shall be colored' indicates a racial component in the composition of the board, which is a characteristic of Jim Crow era legislation aimed at managing or segregating populations.
classification.reasoning: The statute explicitly mandates that two members of the Board of Children's Guardians must be 'colored'. While the primary function of the board is child welfare, the explicit racial quota for its composition is a strong indicator of racial segregation and control mechanisms characteristic of the Jim Crow era. This is not a direct segregation of services, but rather an explicit racial designation in the governing body, which implies a racialized approach to child welfare administration. Therefore, it is classified as Jim Crow. The confidence is high due to the explicit mention of race. The category is 'other' as it doesn't fit neatly into the other provided categories but relates to social welfare and governance.

entries.reviewer_note: Given that it is unlikely that the local government in the counties would choose to hire Black people to serve on the board, the explicit requirement that at least two are hired suggests that this was an attempt to create a board which was less racially biased.

classification.title: GUARDIANS, BOARD OF - FOR CHILDREN IN CERTAIN COUNTIES
classification.summary: This statute outlines the powers and responsibilities of a Board of Children's Guardians in certain counties. It details the conditions under which children can be removed from parental custody (abandonment, neglect, cruelty, begging, parental drunkenness or debauchery, corrupting associations, viciousness, incorrigibility, or unlawful cohabitation). The board is empowered to file petitions in court, take temporary custody of children, and seek final commitment to their guardianship. The court can order parents to pay for the child's support if able. The statute also addresses the board's exemption from court costs and fees, with the county bearing these expenses, and the circuit court's power to remove board members for misconduct.

It establishes a board to oversee these children and outlines the legal processes involved. There is no mention of race or any differential treatment based on race within the text. classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1909 outlines the jurisdiction and procedures for the appointment, removal, and settlement of accounts for guardians of minors. It details which county court has jurisdiction based on the minor's residence, the location of a proven will, or the location of the minor's real or personal estate. It also addresses the consummation of guardianship upon bond execution, the voiding of a second guardian appointment before the first is removed, the scrutiny of settlements between guardians and wards, the prohibition of guardians acquiring conflicting interests, and the domicile of a ward.

It also specifies the appointment and duties of a county health officer. A separate section (§2056) empowers local boards in counties bordering the Ohio and Mississippi rivers, and state lines with West Virginia and Tennessee, to establish quarantines against contagious diseases from other states or counties, with oversight from the State Board of Health.

There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. classification.title: HOUSES OF REFORM
classification.summary: This statute establishes two institutions, one for girls and one for boys, to be known as the House of Reform for Girls and the House of Reform for Boys, respectively. It appropriates $100,000 for their establishment, including purchasing grounds and erecting buildings. The Board of Penitentiary Commissioners is given general supervision and government of these institutions, with the power to appoint subordinate officers, fix salaries, and adopt rules and regulations. The Board is also to appoint a secretary and treasurer, who will hold office for four years and provide bonds. The Board will make an annual report to the Governor. Board members will receive $600 per annum compensation and traveling expenses. Trustees have the power to acquire suitable building sites of at least one hundred acres in healthy locations near a city or town.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the property rights of married women in Kentucky as of 1909. It grants married women the ability to acquire, hold, sell, and dispose of personal property independently, and to make contracts and sue or be sued as if unmarried. However, it restricts their ability to make executory contracts for the sale, conveyance, or mortgage of real estate unless their husband joins them. They retain the right to rent out their real estate and make contracts for its improvement. Transfers of personal property between spouses require written acknowledgment and recording to be valid against third parties. The statute also addresses conveyances of a wife's lands and chattels real by both husband and wife, and notes changes from previous statutes regarding married women's legal status.
classification.reasoning: The statute deals with the property rights of married women and their ability to enter into contracts and manage their property. It does not contain any explicit or implicit references to race or racial segregation. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it appears to be part of a compiled set of statutes from 1909.

classification.title: Husband and Wife - Property Rights
classification.summary: This statute outlines the property rights and liabilities between husbands and wives in Kentucky. It details the husband's limited liability for his wife's debts, the wife's powers in cases of abandonment or lunacy of the husband, and the surviving spouse's inheritance rights in real and personal property. It also includes case law annotations related to these provisions.

classification.summary: This statute section details property rights between husbands and wives, focusing on the husband's right of curtesy in his wife's lands and the wife's right of dower. It outlines conditions under which these rights are acquired, lost (e.g., through divorce or conveyance), and how they are calculated, including provisions for separate estates and trust estates. It also covers the husband's liability for the wife's medical and funeral expenses and the surviving spouse's inheritance rights.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text discusses property rights between husbands and wives, specifically focusing on legal concepts like curtesy and dower. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. The statute appears to be a general civil law concerning marital property rights. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1909 details various aspects of property rights concerning husbands and wives, specifically focusing on dower rights, the sale of land, and inheritance. It covers situations involving widows' rights to clear land, the sale of infant husbands' land, the sale of entire estates when dower cannot be assigned without impairment, sales subject to dower rights, sales under judgments in favor of the state, the requirement of beneficial seizin by the husband for dower, trust estates and dower, the value of dower in alienated land, and a widow's rights when renouncing or taking under a will. The text includes numerous case citations to illustrate legal interpretations.

classification.title: Husband and Wife: Property Rights
classification.summary: This statute outlines procedures for a husband to sell his real estate when his wife is a confirmed lunatic, an infant, or judicially declared an idiot or imbecile. It details how the wife's inchoate right of dower can be conveyed, requiring court approval, covenants for her benefit, and potential involvement of a committee or commissioner. It also addresses a wife's ability to dispose of her estate by will and the reciprocal application of dower provisions to a husband's interest in his wife's real estate.
classification.reasoning: The statute deals with property rights within marriage, specifically concerning the conveyance of real estate when one spouse is incapacitated (lunatic, infant, idiot, imbecile). It outlines legal procedures and protections for the spouse's dower rights. There is no mention of race, and the provisions apply generally to all individuals regardless of race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

§ 2177. **Penalty for wrongfully appropriating property of guest.** That if any inn-keeper shall embezzle or convert to his own use, or fraudulently take, make away with, or secrete, with intent to embezzle or fraudulently convert to his own use, without consent of his guest, any money, bank notes, jewelry, articles of gold or silver manufacture, precious stones or bullion, delivered to such innkeeper by his guest for safe custody, he shall, upon *conviction* thereof, be punished in the manner prescribed by law for feloniously stealing property of the value of the article or articles so embezzled, taken or secreted.

ARTICLE II.

*Houses of Private Entertainment.*

§ 2178. **Charge for entertainment**—when it can not be made. Any person other than the keeper of a tavern or house of private entertainment, who shall entertain in his house another, or furnish him with diet or storage for his goods, not making an agreement for compensation therefor, shall not recover anything against the person so entertained or furnished with diet or storage, or against his estate, but the person so furnishing another shall be considered as doing the same of courtesy. (*See, as to lien of, sec. 2179a.*)

§ 2179. **House of private entertainment**—who deemed keeper of. Any person not a tavern-keeper, who shall furnish for compensation lodging or diet to travelers, or to one boarding in his house, or provender in his stable or on his land for horses or mules, shall be deemed the keeper of a house of private entertainment. No license shall be required to keep a house of private entertainment.

ARTICLE III.

*Lien of Hotel and Boarding-House Keepers.*

§ 2179a. **Lien of hotel and boarding-house keepers**—enforcement of—penalty. 1. That all hotel-keepers, inn-keepers, boarding-house keepers and keepers of houses of private entertainment shall have a lien on all baggage and all personal property owned by, and brought to, such house of entertainment by the person receiving the board, nursing, care or attention from such landlord, for the contract price of such board, care and attention as are received, and in case of no contract price for such board, nursing, care or attention, then for a reasonable price for same.

classification.title: JURIES. Petit Jurors- Qualification and Pay of.
classification.summary: This statute outlines the qualifications and exemptions for petit jurors in Kentucky courts. It specifies age, citizenship, residency, and character requirements. It also lists various professions and roles that are exempt from jury duty, such as civil officers (with exceptions), transient persons, physicians, attorneys, ministers, bank employees, asylum attendants, retail druggists, undertakers, railroad depot agents, and telegraph operators. The statute also addresses juror testimony, penalties for corrupt verdicts, and officer communication with juries. It details challenges for cause and peremptory challenges in civil actions, including grounds for challenge like affinity by marriage, alienage, not being a housekeeper, prior service on a former trial, and partiality. It also clarifies that being a citizen and taxpayer of a city is not a cause for challenge in an action against that city, and that taxpayers and residents of a city are not disqualified to sit in cases involving annexation.

The text focuses on property rights and contractual obligations between landlords and tenants.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text deals with general landlord-tenant law, including lease agreements, rent, and property rights. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial discrimination. The statute appears to be a standard civil law concerning property and contractual relationships. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

The statute also includes case law interpretations regarding conversion to year-to-year tenancies, the status of laborers occupying premises, stipulations for landlord re-entry, tenancies by sufferance, tenancies for less than a year, tenancies with the right to purchase, and tenants in possession for years.

classification.summary: These statutes address property law concerning deeds and inheritances. Section 2351 states that a deed conveying more than the grantor lawfully possesses will convey only what they can lawfully convey. Section 2352 outlines how a purchaser evicted by an heir can recover from the heir to the extent of the estate the heir received from the grantor. Section 2353 clarifies that when a deed is made to one person but the consideration is paid by another, no trust will result in favor of the latter, with specific exceptions for cases where the grantee took the deed without consent or in violation of a trust. The annotations provide case law examples and interpretations of these sections.

It mandates the appraisement of real estate before such sales by two disinterested housekeepers, with the officer acting as umpire if they disagree. The text also includes a section on trespass, stating that actual possession is not necessary to maintain an action for damages or to prevent injury to land.

There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. classification.title: Fraudulent certification of land titles.
classification.summary: This statute, enacted in 1904 and appearing in the 1909 Kentucky Statutes, addresses fraudulent certification of land titles. It makes it unlawful for county court clerks or other officers to certify abstracts or statements of title under specific circumstances, such as when the land is in the actual possession of someone other than the person shown as the owner by the abstract, and the possessor claims under an adverse title. classification.title: Limitation of Actions
classification.summary: This statute outlines the time limits for bringing various civil actions. It specifies that actions for personal injury, injury to property by railroads, malicious prosecution, libel, slander, escape of prisoners, and recovery of usury must be commenced within one year of the cause of action accruing. It also provides specific limitations for actions related to death by wrongful act, burning property by fire from trains, false imprisonment, malpractice, seduction, and stock killed by railroads. The statute also addresses when the right to recover usury accrues and the procedural requirements for pleading the statute of limitations.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text deals with the limitations of actions in civil cases, specifying the timeframes within which lawsuits must be filed for various types of claims. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. The statute appears to be a general procedural law applicable to all citizens. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it is presented as part of a compiled statute collection (Kentucky Statutes 1909).

For merchant's accounts, actions must be brought within two years, with the limitation computed from the first day of January succeeding the delivery of articles. classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1909 outlines the limitations of actions related to streets, alleys, and public roads. It specifies when the statute of limitations begins to run for a city to recover a street or alley, requiring written notification from the party in possession that their possession is adverse to the city's right. Until such notice, possession is deemed amicable, and the possessor is considered a tenant at will of the city. It also includes provisions for suspending statutes of limitations due to injunctions, lawful restraints, vacancies in office, absence of an officer, or refusal to act, and for commencing new actions after a dismissal for lack of jurisdiction.

It also addresses bond requirements for repeat offenders, the legality of C.O.D. shipments, and exceptions for manufacturers, wholesale dealers, druggists (under specific conditions and prescriptions), and physicians. The statute specifies that it does not apply to manufacturers or wholesale dealers selling in quantities of not less than five gallons, delivered at one time, not to be drunk on the premises. Druggists can sell for medical purposes with a physician's prescription, provided the election notice specified this exception. Physicians are penalized for issuing fraudulent prescriptions.

There is no explicit or implicit mention of race or any discriminatory provisions targeting a specific racial group. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. classification.summary: This statute prohibits the sale or distribution of intoxicating liquors in counties, districts, precincts, towns, or cities where such sales are prohibited by special act or local option vote. It outlines exceptions for individuals bringing liquor for private use (up to one gallon) and for licensed physicians and druggists receiving up to five gallons in unbroken packages. The law also defines each package as a separate offense, sets penalties, and states that the place of delivery is considered the place of sale. It specifically applies to common carriers and those who carry freight or goods for hire and receive payment for conveying liquors. A separate section addresses tricks or devices to evade these laws.
classification.reasoning: The statute addresses the prohibition and regulation of intoxicating liquors in areas where sales are banned by local option or special acts. While it deals with the sale and distribution of alcohol, it does not contain any explicit or implicit racial components. The regulations apply universally to all individuals and entities within the specified local option territories, regardless of race. Therefore, it is not classified as a Jim Crow law. classification.title: State Guard Companies - Organization and Eligibility
classification.summary: This statute outlines the process for organizing State Guard companies in Kentucky. It specifies that the Governor can authorize the formation of such companies when deemed necessary. It also details the requirements for individuals wishing to join, including a minimum of forty and a maximum of eighty members per company, written consent from the county judge, a certificate of good moral character and residency, and the Governor's approval. Eligibility for membership is extended to able-bodied male residents between eighteen and forty-five years old, of sound mind and good moral character, residing within the county. Provisions are also made for individuals between fifteen and eighteen years old to become eligible with parental consent. The statute also mentions that once a company is organized and has adopted by-laws, recruits may be subject to additional qualifications set by those by-laws.

It details the requirements for passing an examination, including moral character, sobriety, knowledge of mining practices and gases, and a minimum of five years of practical experience. A 'service certificate' is also provided for individuals with prior experience as a mine foreman or assistant foreman. The statute also establishes a Board of Examiners composed of the Chief Inspector and two assistants.
classification.reasoning: The statute pertains to the qualifications and examination of mine inspectors and foremen in coal mines. It sets standards for experience, knowledge, and character. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial discrimination. The focus is solely on professional qualifications for mine safety and operation. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is inferred as 'codes' because it appears to be part of a compiled set of statutes (Kentucky Statutes 1909).

classification.title: Payment of mining employes
classification.summary: This statute mandates that employers in the mining industry must pay their employees in lawful U.S. currency on or before the 15th and 30th of each month. It also prohibits employers from coercing employees to trade at a particular store, which is referred to as blacklisting. Employees absent at the time of payment are entitled to receive their wages upon demand thereafter.
classification.reasoning: The statute addresses labor practices in the mining industry, specifically concerning the payment of wages and preventing coercive trade practices. There is no mention of race or any differential treatment based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document appears to be part of a compiled code of laws, as indicated by the chapter and section numbering and the reference to amendments.

It also mentions an appropriation for a statue of Henry Clay. The text also includes a separate, unrelated statute from 1898 concerning employer-employee relations and prohibiting company stores or blacklisting for failure to patronize specific establishments.

While this could potentially have been used in a discriminatory manner, the text itself does not explicitly mention race or any discriminatory intent. The second section (§2739e and related subsections) concerns the appropriation of funds for the erection of statues of historical figures (William Goebel and Henry Clay). classification.title: MOTOR VEHICLES
classification.summary: This statute, enacted on March 26, 1904, establishes regulations for motor vehicle operation on public highways in Kentucky. It sets speed limits, with a general maximum of 15 miles per hour, and lower limits (6 miles per hour) for specific hazardous areas like crossings, bridges, sharp curves, and steep descents. It also mandates that operators give audible warning when approaching pedestrians or animals, take precautions to ensure their safety, and reduce speed or stop if necessary. The statute aims to prevent accidents and ensure public safety on roadways.

There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. classification.summary: This statute outlines the establishment and governance of a Free Public Library within municipal corporations of the first class. It details the appointment of trustees, their qualifications, the powers and duties of the Board of Trustees, meeting procedures, financial management, and the levying of taxes for library maintenance. The mayor is a trustee ex officio. Trustees are unpaid, must be taxpayers and qualified voters residing in the city for two years. The board can make rules, contract, sue and be sued, acquire property, erect buildings, and manage library affairs. Funds are deposited in a chartered bank and withdrawn by check. A tax of 2.5 to 4 cents per $100 of assessed property can be levied for the library.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the process for the dedication and acceptance of public ways (streets and alleys) within a city. It details procedures for closing streets or alleys, including the requirement for owner consent or court approval based on benefit to the city and lack of injury to non-consenting parties. It also addresses the original construction costs of streets, roads, lanes, alleys, or avenues, specifying that these costs are borne by the owners of lots in each fourth of a square, appointed by the Board of Public Works based on the number of square feet owned. The statute also includes case law references regarding the right to alley use by user, agreements to keep streets in repair, the benefit to owners and public need for improvements, the delegation of municipal authority, curing invalid assessments, and double taxation.
classification.reasoning: The statute pertains to municipal corporations and the regulation of public ways (streets and alleys). It details procedures for the dedication, acceptance, and closing of these ways, as well as the cost allocation for their original construction. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial segregation or discrimination. The statute appears to be a general civil or administrative law concerning urban infrastructure and property rights. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

There is no mention of race, nor any provisions that would implicitly discriminate based on race. The focus is purely on property ownership and the apportionment of costs for public infrastructure. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

It details exemptions from military and jury duty for police officers, restrictions on political affiliations for police, and the disciplinary procedures for fire department members under the control of a board of public safety. It also specifies that members of the fire department cannot be fined, reprimanded, removed, suspended, or dismissed without written charges and a hearing, with an exception for those who become insane or of unsound mind.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text (Section 2896-96a) pertains to the organization, discipline, and operational regulations of police and fire departments in first-class cities in Kentucky. It covers aspects like exemptions from duty, political affiliations, and disciplinary procedures for department members. There is no mention of race, segregation, or any differential treatment based on race. Therefore, it does not appear to be a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it is presented as part of a compiled statute book (Kentucky Statutes 1909).

classification.summary: This statute outlines the powers and responsibilities of the board of public safety in first-class cities regarding the fire department. It details the board's authority to summon witnesses, conduct trials, and render judgments on charges against fire department members. It also specifies the board's role in providing equipment, engine houses, and accommodations for the fire department, and lists the required officers and their minimum salaries.
classification.reasoning: The statute describes the organization and operation of a fire department in first-class cities. It details the powers of the board of public safety, the provision of equipment, and the salaries of fire department personnel. There is no mention of race or any provisions that would suggest racial segregation or discrimination. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: Municipal Corporations - First Class - Police and Fire Department
classification.summary: This statute outlines the organization and management of the police and fire departments for first-class municipal corporations. It details staffing requirements, salary minimums for various positions within the fire department (mechanic, painter, pipemen, linemen, battery-man, harnessmaker, substitute firemen), procedures for increasing firemen numbers, appointment and qualification criteria for fire department members (chief, assistant chief, captains), and disciplinary actions for offenses, including reprimand, pay forfeiture, suspension, and dismissal. It also covers deductions from salary for absences and establishes that five consecutive days of absence without leave or total disability constitutes a resignation.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text details the operational structure, staffing, qualifications, and disciplinary procedures for municipal police and fire departments. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial segregation or discrimination. The statute focuses solely on the administrative and operational aspects of these public services. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the organization, compensation, privileges, and pension fund for fire departments in first-class cities. It details the composition of the board of trustees for the firemen's pension fund, the taxation for the fund, and the investment of these funds. It also specifies privileges for firemen, such as exemption from military or jury duty and arrest on civil process while on duty, and grants fire apparatus the right of way on streets. Penalties for obstructing fire apparatus are also mentioned.
classification.reasoning: The statute pertains to the operational aspects of fire departments in first-class cities, including employee compensation, privileges, and a pension fund. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial segregation or discrimination. The statute focuses on the organization and benefits for fire department personnel without any racial dimension. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: Firemen's Pension Fund
classification.summary: This statute outlines the establishment and management of a firemen's pension fund in first-class cities. It details how the fund is financed through assessments on members' salaries, fines, rewards, and taxes. The board of public safety is designated as the trustee, responsible for managing and investing the fund. The statute specifies who is eligible to receive pensions (disabled members, their widows, and dependent children under fourteen, or dependent parents) and the conditions for receiving them, including temporary total disability. It also details the powers of the pension board regarding rules, regulations, and decision-making on pension applications.
classification.reasoning: The statute concerns the establishment and administration of a pension fund for fire department members. It details financial contributions, management by a board, and eligibility for benefits. There is no mention of race or any provisions that would implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it appears to be part of a compiled statute collection (Kentucky Statutes 1909).

The provisions apply to all members of the fire department regardless of their race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: Municipal Corporations - Comptroller
classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1909 outlines the appointment, duties, and powers of a Comptroller in municipal corporations of the first class. The Comptroller is appointed by the mayor with the approval of the board of aldermen and is responsible for overseeing the city's fiscal affairs, including the collection and disbursement of revenues, ensuring proper accounting, preventing unauthorized expenditures, and maintaining financial records. The Comptroller also has custody of the city seal and public records and must provide an annual report on the city's financial condition.

classification.title: Police Court Jurisdiction and Powers
classification.summary: This statute outlines the jurisdiction and powers of the Police Court in first-class cities. It details the court's role as an examining court for felonies and misdemeanors, the procedures for reporting testimony in felony cases, and the court's authority to commit or discharge accused individuals, set bonds, and transmit case papers. It also specifies penalties, including fines and imprisonment (not exceeding thirty days), and the possibility of hard labor. The statute further addresses cases involving the custody of children, drunkenness, and disorderly conduct, including the imposition of fines and the requirement of peace bonds. It also touches upon the practice and rules of the court for ordinance violations and state statute violations.

It details how cases are handled, what penalties can be imposed, and the court's general authority. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial segregation or discrimination. The penalties and procedures described appear to apply generally to all individuals brought before the court. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

**§ 2975. Eligibility to office of trustee.** No person shall be eligible to the office of trustee of the public schools who has not attained the age of thirty years, and who is not a housekeeper, or is not the owner of real estate in said city, or who is not a citizen of the United States, or a *bona fide* resident of the Commonwealth of Kentucky and of the legislative district of the city for which he is elected, for three years next preceding his election; or who holds or discharges any office, deputyship, or agency under the city, or any district or county, or under the State of Kentucky or any department thereof, or under the United States or any foreign government, except notaries public and militia officers of Kentucky. No person shall be eligible to this office who, at the time of his election, is directly or indirectly interested in any contract with the board, or who holds any office of trust, agency, or salary with any corporation which holds any contract with the board, or who is in any way benefited by the appropriations of the board; or whose father, son, brother, wife, daughter, or sister is employed as teacher or as professor, or in any other capacity by said board, or in any of the public schools, or who is, directly or indirectly, interested in the sale to the board of books, stationery, or other property.

**§ 2976. Member becoming disqualified—office vacated.** If, after election, any member of the board should become a candidate for nomination or for any office or agency, the holding and discharging of which would have rendered him ineligible before his election, or should he remove out of the district for which he was chosen, or should he do or incur anything which would have rendered him ineligible for election, or should any of the relatives above specified be employed by the board, his office shall become vacant and be filled as herein directed.

**§ 2977. Members privileged in debate.** Members of the board shall not be elsewhere called in question for language used in debate.

**§ 2978. Separation of white and colored children.** No white child shall become a pupil in any school for colored children, and no colored child shall become a pupil in any school for white children; but schools for white and colored children shall be kept and maintained separately.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the revenue and taxation powers of first-class municipal corporations in Kentucky. It details how cities can levy taxes on personal property, licenses, and franchises, and specifies that ad valorem taxes must be imposed on certain public utility properties. The statute also mandates that taxes and license fees must be levied by ordinance, with the purpose clearly stated, and the revenue used only for that specified purpose. It further clarifies the collection methods for different types of taxes and references various court cases and constitutional sections related to municipal taxation.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text deals with municipal revenue and taxation powers. It outlines the legal framework for how cities can collect taxes on various forms of property and licenses. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. The statute's focus is purely on the financial and administrative aspects of municipal governance. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: Liquor Licenses
classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1909 outlines regulations for liquor licenses. It specifies that there will be only one form of license for retailing liquor, with the tax determined by the general council, ranging from $150 to $1000. The license authorizes the sale of vinous, spirituous, or malt liquors. It defines retailers as those selling less than five gallons, while wholesale dealers can sell cases of bottled liquor (at least two gallons) to non-residents for consumption outside the city. Druggists and apothecaries are permitted to sell unmixed alcohol or admixtures of liquors for medicinal purposes or upon a physician's prescription, but not as a beverage. They must require a separate prescription for each sale.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text details regulations concerning liquor licenses, including tax amounts, definitions of retailers and wholesalers, and provisions for druggists and apothecaries. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial segregation or discrimination. Therefore, this statute is not classified as a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the process for municipal corporations to annex unincorporated territory or reduce their boundaries. It details the requirements for enacting ordinances, publishing notices, and the conditions under which annexation or reduction becomes effective. It also addresses the annexation of other cities of the second, third, or fourth class, requiring a voter referendum. A specific provision (§ 3050b) deals with the rights of taxpayers in annexed unincorporated territory regarding school buildings, ensuring they receive credit for prior contributions towards grounds and buildings.

There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial segregation or discrimination. The focus is purely on the administrative and legal aspects of city expansion and the financial implications for residents of newly incorporated areas. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

It also includes a specific clause regarding the sale of liquor in annexed unincorporated territories if voters there had previously prohibited it.
classification.reasoning: The statute details the legal procedures for municipal annexation in Kentucky. It covers financial liabilities, property rights, and the integration of new residents into the city's electoral system. While it mentions the prohibition of liquor sales based on prior local votes, there is no explicit or implicit mention of race or any discriminatory intent towards any racial group. Therefore, it is not classified as a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: Kentucky Statutes 1909, Chapter 89, Sections 3055-3058
classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1909, specifically Chapter 89, Sections 3055-3058, outlines the general powers of municipal corporations of the second class. It details regulations regarding the redistricting or changing of wards, including qualifications of voters and the timing of such changes. It also grants the general council powers to enact ordinances, including those related to quarantine and health, quarries, and the destruction of diseased food or drink. The text also includes case law annotations related to actions and remedies against cities, writ of prohibition, authority to sell and convey, contracts with bridge companies, and the council's power to abolish offices.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text deals with the administrative and general powers of municipal corporations, specifically concerning the division of cities into wards, voter qualifications, and the council's authority to pass ordinances related to public health and other municipal matters. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: Municipal Corporations - Street Improvements
classification.summary: This statute grants general councils exclusive control over city streets, roadways, sidewalks, alleys, landings, wharves, public grounds, and highways. It outlines powers related to establishing, altering, widening, closing, grading, paving, cleaning, and repairing these areas. It also covers preventing encroachments, installing drains and sewers, regulating vaults and areas under sidewalks, and enforcing connections with utility mains. The statute further details provisions for sprinkling districts, actions to recover streets, condemnation of property for street purposes, dedication of land for public use, easements in streets, injury by grading, street lighting contracts, and liability for accidents in streets or at wharves.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text pertains to the general powers and responsibilities of municipal corporations regarding street improvements and public grounds. It details the administrative and legal aspects of managing urban infrastructure. There is no mention of race, racial classifications, or any provisions that would suggest discriminatory practices based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it appears to be part of a compiled set of statutes from 1909, likely a revision or codification of existing laws.

It also covers the condemnation of land for public purposes and the apportionment of costs for street and sidewalk construction and reconstruction.

classification.title: Municipal Corporations - Elections
classification.summary: This statute outlines the election and terms of office for various municipal officers in second-class cities, including the mayor, city clerk, treasurer, attorney, solicitor, engineer, assessor, jailer, and members of the board of aldermen and councilmen. It also specifies the qualifications for voters, requiring them to be male inhabitants, 21 years of age or older, citizens of Kentucky, bona fide residents of the city for six months, residents of the precinct for sixty days, and registered voters. The statute details the election schedule for the police court judge and the process for determining the terms of council members. It also includes a section on the qualifications for a civil engineer candidate.
classification.reasoning: The statute details the election process and qualifications for municipal officers and voters in second-class cities. While it specifies voter qualifications such as age, citizenship, residency, and registration, it does not contain any explicit or implicit racial distinctions. The term 'male inhabitants' refers to gender, not race. Therefore, this statute is not classified as a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the process for assessing real and personal property for taxation in second-class cities in Kentucky. It details quadrennial assessments for real property, annual assessments for personal property, and provisions for correcting valuations due to new structures or destruction. It also authorizes the general council to levy ad valorem taxes, poll taxes, and license fees for various purposes, specifying that ordinances must clearly state the purpose of the levy and that revenue must be expended accordingly. It includes provisions for officer liability in case of improper expenditure.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the fiscal year, property assessment procedures, and the election and duties of assessors for municipal corporations of the second class in Kentucky. It details the timing of assessments, the requirement for fair cash value, and penalties for failure to assess property subject to city taxation. The fiscal year ends on December 31st, and property is assessed as of September 1st for the following year's taxes. Assessors are elected for four-year terms and must meet specific qualifications, including being a homeowner and voter in the city. Penalties are outlined for assessors who knowingly fail to assess taxable property.

It sets forth the fiscal year, the dates for property assessment, and the qualifications and responsibilities of assessors. The language and subject matter are purely administrative and financial, related to the functioning of local government. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the process for redeeming real estate sold for unpaid taxes in third-class cities. classification.title: Third Class- Board of Public Works
classification.summary: This statute outlines the organization and powers of the Board of Public Works in third-class cities. It details the eligibility of board members, their participation in city council proceedings, their exclusive right to employ and remove department heads (firemen, workhouse, hospital, almshouse, city prison employees, engineers, clerks, superintendents, scavengers), and their authority to fix salaries. It also specifies that the board cannot employ individuals related to board members, the mayor, or council members within the third degree of consanguinity or affinity. Furthermore, the statute grants the board exclusive control over public ways, places, and property, including construction, maintenance, and improvements of streets, parks, public buildings, and utilities. It also details their power to make expenditures under a certain threshold and to let contracts over a specified amount to the lowest bidder. A separate section discusses the powers of a water company and the city's authority in determining qualifications for water connections.

classification.title: Municipal Corporations - Streets and Alleys
classification.summary: This statute outlines the regulations for municipal corporations in Kentucky regarding the cost and assessment of street and alley improvements. It specifies that the cost to property owners should not exceed half the value of their lots, with provisions for valuation if disputed. It also details exemptions from repair costs for property owners after initial improvements, with exceptions for sidewalks, curbs, and gutters, and outlines the mayor's authority to order and enforce repairs. The city is responsible for the cost of improving street intersections. The common council has the power to grade, construct, and repair streets, sidewalks, and alleys, and can allocate city funds for these improvements. Courts can correct mistakes made by engineers or the council in these matters.
classification.reasoning: The statute deals with municipal improvements, specifically streets and alleys, and the financial responsibilities of property owners and the city. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial discrimination. The regulations appear to be purely administrative and financial concerning public works. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the powers and jurisdiction of a city court judge in a fourth-class municipal corporation. It details the judge's authority as a conservator of the peace, their power to order arrests, require bail, and handle various offenses including those against state laws and city ordinances. The court has examining jurisdiction for most cases (except homicide), concurrent jurisdiction with justices of the peace for certain offenses, and civil jurisdiction co-extensive with the county. It lists specific misdemeanors like affrays, riots, breaches of the peace, indecent or immoral behavior, drunkenness, and carrying concealed weapons, for which fines or imprisonment may be prescribed by ordinance. The judge also has exclusive jurisdiction over offenses arising from city ordinances and the power to issue summons, compel witness attendance, and punish contempt. The statute also covers the judge's role as clerk, the appointment of a deputy clerk, and the taxation of judge's costs in trials.
classification.reasoning: The statute describes the judicial functions of a city court. It details the powers of the judge, the types of cases they can hear, and procedural aspects of the court. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial discrimination. The offenses listed are general and do not appear to be targeted at any specific racial group. Therefore, it is classified as not a Jim Crow law.

§ 3526. Fines and forfeitures- collection. All fines and forfeitures recov
ered shall be collected by the chief of police , or other officer to whom exe-
cution or capias pro fine is directed , and shall be paid by him to the city
treasurer ; but before the issual of final process the defendant may pay
the fine or forfeiture to the chief of police , who shall pay it to the treas
urer as aforesaid .
§ 3527. Attachment upon return of execution. A return " not found " on a
capias pro fine and of " no property found " on a writ of fieri facias issued
on any judgment in the said court , shall authorize an attachment in favor
of the Commonwealth , or of the city against the choses in action or effects
of the defendants or defendant , in the same manner that a return of "n
property found " authorizes an attachment in equity on judgment in the
circuit court .
§ 3528. Fines- executions confinement - hard labor- replevy. Upon all judg
ments of fines rendered by the city court , whether in favor of the Com
monwealth or for the city , it shall be lawful for the city attorney to cause
a fi.fa . to be issued , to be levied on the estate of the defendant , or to take
a capias pro fine , requiring the imprisonment of the defendant in the city
workhouse , if there be one , or the county jail , or confined at work upon
the streets of said city or in said workhouse , at the rate of one dollar
per day until the fine and costs are paid , unless such rate of wages shall
be changed by the board of council ; and when any fine or costs shallbe
paid by labor , the city shall not be liable to any officer for any part of
such fine or cost . The defendant may at any time replevy said finefor
three months by executing a bond , with good surety thereon , for amount
of fine and costs and six per cent interest thereon .
§ 3529. Witnesses ' fees taxed as costs. Witnesses in penal cases shallbe
allowed the same fees as are allowed witnesses in circuit courts , to be
taxed as costs , and to be payable only in cases where judgment goes
against the defendant and is collected .
§ 3530. Trial with or without jury- bond to keep the peace . In all cases where
persons are presented to said court , charged with an offense within its
jurisdiction , the judge may hear and determine the case , and impose such
fines without the intervention of a jury ; but in all cases where the fine
may be more than twenty dollars , the defendant may demand that the
issue of fact be tried by a jury ; and in all cases of drunkenness or dis
orderly conduct , in addition to imposing a fine , he may hold the offender
to bail in any sum , not exceeding one thousand dollars , to keep the peace
and be of good behavior for any length of time , not exceeding one year.
or he may impose the fine without holding to bail ; and thereupon the
offender shall be forthwith committed to the workhouse , stationhouse or
county jail , and shall there be kept in custody until the bail is given or
the time for which it was required shall have expired , and until the fine
and costs are paid or replevied , or satisfied by labor as provided by law.

§ 3533. Assessment - when to make - duties in relation to. It shall be the duty
of the assessor , on or before the first Monday in May of each year , to take
