classification.summary: This statute outlines the powers and responsibilities of the board of education in fourth-class municipal corporations regarding public schools. It covers aspects such as the board's autonomy in managing its officers, teachers, and employees; the acquisition and disposition of school property; the selection of textbooks and curriculum; the establishment of various school types (high schools, kindergartens, manual training schools); and financial reporting. They are also required to publish an annual statement on school conditions and finances.

classification.title: Public Schools - Fourth Class Municipal Corporations
classification.summary: This statute outlines the organization and funding of public schools in fourth-class cities. It details the appropriation of funds, the election and duties of the board of education and its secretary, the establishment of school libraries, the admission of pupils from outside city limits with tuition fees, and the distribution of state school funds. Crucially, section 3606 explicitly states that the Superintendent of Public Instruction shall pay state school funds to the 'white board of education' for white children and to the 'colored board of education' for colored children, at the same per capita rate as other districts. This explicit segregation of school boards and per capita funding based on race clearly indicates a Jim Crow law.

It specifies that voter qualifications in municipal elections should align with state election laws, except where otherwise provided. It also details procedures for towns where registration is not required, including the use of separate ballot boxes, and addresses voting rights for residents of towns located in multiple counties.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text pertains to municipal corporations, specifically focusing on annexation, condemnation of property, and elections. The sections on elections (§ 3669, § 3670, § 3670a) detail voter qualifications, registration requirements, ballot box procedures, and voting rights for residents of towns spanning multiple counties. There is no mention of race or any provisions that would implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. Therefore, this statute is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the appointment, duties, and compensation of patrols in Kentucky counties. County courts are authorized to divide counties into districts and appoint patrols to maintain public peace and order. Patrols are tasked with visiting suspected places and places of unlawful assemblies. Compensation is based on hours of service, with a higher rate for counties with over 150,000 inhabitants. A separate section addresses the appointment of patrolmen in counties with first-class cities, with compensation paid by petitioners or employers.
classification.reasoning: The statute itself does not explicitly mention race. However, the historical context of 'patrols' in the Jim Crow era strongly suggests their use in enforcing racial segregation and controlling Black populations. Patrols were often used to monitor the movement and activities of Black individuals, particularly at night, and to prevent 'unlawful assemblies' which could include any gathering of Black people. Therefore, while not explicit, the function of these patrols is implicitly tied to the enforcement of Jim Crow laws. The higher compensation in larger counties might also hint at a greater need for such enforcement in more populous, and thus potentially more diverse, areas. Due to the implicit nature and the need for historical context to fully understand its application, human review is recommended.

classification.summary: This statute, Section 3828 of the Kentucky Statutes of 1909, outlines the powers and procedures for the State Board of Prison Commissioners to grant paroles to convicted felons. It specifies conditions for parole, including the exclusion of individuals convicted of rape or incest, those with prior felony convictions, or those who have been insubordinate. The statute details the process of granting parole, the conditions under which a paroled convict remains under the control of the warden and the Board, and the authority to retake and re-imprison parolees. It also designates the written order of the Board as sufficient warrant for law enforcement officers to arrest and deliver parolees back to the penitentiary.
classification.reasoning: The statute deals with the parole system for convicted felons in Kentucky. It outlines the authority of the State Board of Prison Commissioners to grant paroles, the conditions for eligibility, and the process for re-imprisonment. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly discriminate based on race. classification.title: Kentucky Statutes 1909, Chapter 98: Personal Representatives - General Provisions
classification.summary: This statute outlines the general provisions for personal representatives in Kentucky, specifically detailing the order of payment for debts and liabilities of a decedent's estate. It establishes that debts owed to a personal representative for the estate of a deceased person, ward, or person of unsound mind held by the decedent shall be paid in full before any pro rata distributions. All other debts and liabilities are of equal dignity and are to be paid ratably. The statute also addresses the process for verifying claims against a decedent's estate, requiring written affidavits from the claimant or their agent, and in some cases, a secondary affidavit from another person attesting to the claim's validity. It also details how liens on estate property are handled, with proceeds first applied to discharge the lien, and any remaining debt receiving a pro rata share.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text deals with the administration of estates, the payment of debts, and the verification of claims against a decedent's estate. There is no mention of race, racial classifications, or any provisions that would suggest discriminatory practices based on race. The statute appears to be a general procedural law concerning probate and estate management. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This statute establishes a lien on property for taxes owed to the Commonwealth, county, incorporated city, town, or taxing district. The lien is valid for five years and cannot be defeated by gift, devise, sale, or alienation unless it occurred more than five years before enforcement proceedings. Nothing is exempt from levy and sale for taxes and associated costs. The statute also allows for retrospective assessment of unassessed lands or improvements within five years, but this does not prejudice the rights of purchasers acquired in the meantime. It also defines real estate and personal property for taxation purposes.

It also addresses procedures for re-assessment in cases where tax books or schedules are lost or destroyed.

classification.title: Assessment of Railroads - Distribution of School Funds
classification.summary: This statute outlines the assessment of railroad taxes and the subsequent distribution of these funds for school purposes. Specifically, it mandates that taxes collected within a school district shall be held by the county superintendent as a graded or common school fund. This fund is then to be apportioned between white graded common schools or white common school districts and any colored common school districts located within the same boundary. The distribution ratio is based on the proportion of white children of pupil age and colored children of pupil age residing in the district compared to the total number of children, white and colored, residing in the district where the tax is collected.
classification.reasoning: The statute explicitly mentions the distribution of school funds between 'white graded common school or white common school district' and 'any colored common school district'. This direct reference to separate educational facilities based on race, and the mechanism for distributing funds between them, clearly indicates a Jim Crow-era law related to education. The confidence is high because the racial distinction is explicit and the context is educational funding, a common area for Jim Crow legislation. It levies a tax on property transferred by deed, grant, sale, or gift, made in contemplation of death or intended to take effect after death. Certain close relatives (father, mother, husband, wife, lawful issue, etc.) and adopted children are exempt from this tax. The tax rate is five dollars on every hundred dollars of fair cash value, with exemptions for the first five hundred dollars of an estate. It also details procedures for appraising estates in remainder or reversion and allows for bonds to be executed for deferred tax payments.

It also details provisions for counties with low assessed valuations to vote on additional road taxes, the appointment of road overseers, requirements for labor, and reporting obligations. The statute emphasizes that funds collected must be spent within the district where the tax originates and includes provisions for penalties for fraudulent reports. It also allows for the requirement of able-bodied road hands to perform labor as directed by the fiscal court and outlines the process for holding elections to determine public wishes on road taxes.

Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it appears to be part of a compiled statute collection (Kentucky Statutes 1909).

It details responsibilities for opening, widening, changing, and inspecting roads, as well as ensuring they are kept clear of obstructions. The statute also covers the use of funds for road work, the period for road grading, reporting contractor failures, and alternative methods for road maintenance, including the use of delinquent taxpayers and persons sentenced to labor. The statute also allows for the county judge to oversee road work if a supervisor is not appointed.

It details the roles and responsibilities of supervisors and fiscal courts, including the use of labor from delinquent taxpayers and individuals sentenced to labor. While it mentions the use of 'balls and chains on convicts to prevent their escape,' this is a general penal measure and not explicitly tied to racial discrimination. There is no mention of race or any differential treatment based on race. Therefore, this statute is not classified as a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This section outlines the general provisions for common schools in Kentucky, including the requirement for a uniform system, the definition of a common school, and the apportionment of the school fund. It also includes case law annotations regarding the exclusion of negro children from school funds and the teaching of higher branches.
classification.reasoning: The statute itself, 'Ch.113] [§ 4363-4SCHOOLS - COMMON . General Provisions .', does not explicitly mention race. However, the annotations under §4364 are crucial. Annotation (2) states: '(2) An act excluding negro children from any share of the proceeds of the common school fund, as well as from the annual tax levied on the property of white persons for school purposes, was held unconstitutional in Dawson v. Lee, 83 Ky., 49; 6 R., 413.' This annotation directly references an act that excluded 'negro children' from school funds, which is a clear indicator of Jim Crow-era racial segregation in education. While the main text of §4363 and §4364 focuses on the general provisions of common schools, the inclusion of this annotation within the 1909 compilation of statutes strongly suggests that the context of these statutes, even if not explicitly stated in the primary text, was influenced by or dealing with racial segregation. The presence of 'colored schools' and 'separate schools for white and colored' in the table of contents (though not fully provided in the excerpt) further supports this classification. Therefore, the statute is classified as Jim Crow due to the explicit mention of racial exclusion in the accompanying legal commentary and the implied context of racial separation in the broader chapter structure.

classification.title: Common School Fund
classification.summary: These statutes outline the management and allocation of Kentucky's common school fund. They specify that the fund shall not be used for any purpose other than the expenses of the State Department of Education and in aid of common schools. The primary use of the fund is for the payment of legally qualified and employed teachers. The Auditor is responsible for maintaining accounts and ensuring proper distribution to counties, while the Superintendent of Public Instruction estimates per-pupil shares. Provisions are made for handling deficits and surpluses. Incidental expenses like fees are to be paid from the county levy, not the distributable school revenue.
classification.reasoning: The provided statutes (Sections 4371-4375) detail the financial administration and distribution of Kentucky's common school fund. The text focuses on the procedural aspects of managing educational funds, including who can access the funds (expenses of the Department of Education and payment of teachers), how accounts are managed (by the Auditor), and how funds are distributed (by the Superintendent of Public Instruction to counties). There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial segregation or discrimination. The language is purely administrative and financial concerning the education system. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the qualifications, examination process, and election procedures for county superintendents in Kentucky. It specifies eligibility requirements, including not holding certain other offices, and details the examination administered by the State Board of Examiners. A key provision states that in counties with a first-class city maintaining a separate school system, only residents outside that city are eligible for county superintendent. The statute was amended in March 1894.
classification.reasoning: The statute concerns the election and qualifications of county superintendents. While it does not explicitly mention race, the provision stating that 'In counties embracing any city of the first class, maintaining a system of public schools separate and distinct from the common schools of the county, no person shall be eligible to the office of county superintendent other than a resident of such county, outside of such city or town' is a strong implicit indicator of Jim Crow era practices. This type of clause was often used to segregate educational administration and leadership, particularly in areas with significant Black populations and separate school systems. The 'separate and distinct' school system for cities of the first class is a direct reference to the dual school systems common under Jim Crow. Therefore, it is classified as Jim Crow with implicit racial indicators. The confidence is high due to the clear reference to separate school systems and residency restrictions tied to them. classification.summary: This statute outlines the election, duties, and bond requirements for County Superintendents in Kentucky. It specifies the term of office, the process for election and certification, and the responsibilities of the Superintendent in managing school districts, including the power to abolish or change districts and condemn dilapidated schoolhouses. A key provision states that in counties with cities of the first or second class maintaining separate public school systems, the county superintendent must reside outside such cities and be elected by voters residing outside those cities.
keywords: cities of the first or second class
classification.reasoning: The statute itself does not explicitly mention race. However, the provision stating that 'in counties containing cities of the first or second class maintaining a system of public schools separate and distinct from the common schools of the county, the county superintendent shall reside in the portion of the county outside of such city, or cities, and be elected by the qualified voters of said county residing outside of such city or cities' is highly suggestive of segregation. Historically, cities of the first and second class in Kentucky often had significant Black populations, and separate school systems were a hallmark of Jim Crow. This provision implicitly creates a separate electoral and administrative sphere for the common schools based on residency outside of these urban centers, which likely correlated with racial demographics and the maintenance of separate educational facilities. While not explicitly discriminatory on its face, its historical context strongly implies a racial dimension in its application. Therefore, it is classified as 'implicit' racial indicator. The confidence is high because the language about separate school systems and distinct electoral bases for the superintendent strongly points to the context of racial segregation, even without explicit mention of race. The category is 'education' as it directly pertains to the administration of common schools.

classification.title: Seminary property may be acquired by trustees.
classification.summary: This statute authorizes trustees holding legal title to county seminary property (acquired before December 18, 1865) to sell, transfer, or convey it to the trustees of white common school districts where the seminary property is located. The proceeds or property must be used for the education of white pupils, with provisions for white pupils from other districts to receive a reduction to compensate for their interest in the seminary property.
classification.reasoning: The statute explicitly mentions 'white common school districts' and 'white pupils,' indicating a racial segregation in the educational system. The transfer of seminary property is specifically directed towards schools for white children, and any compensation for other districts is framed in terms of 'white pupils.' This clearly falls under Jim Crow legislation related to education. The document type is 'codes' as it is presented as a section within a compiled statute book (Kentucky Statutes 1909).

classification.title: Levy and collection of tax for school indebtedness
classification.summary: This statute, § 4442, states that a tax levied to pay indebtedness for schoolhouses shall be collected as provided by law for the present school tax. However, it includes a proviso that 'no tax shall be levied or collected from the property of colored persons to pay any indebtedness incurred for the benefit of schools for white children.'
classification.reasoning: The statute explicitly mentions 'colored persons' and 'white children' in the context of taxation for schoolhouse indebtedness. This clearly indicates a racial distinction in the application of the tax, which is a hallmark of Jim Crow legislation. The proviso exempts the property of colored persons from being taxed to pay for schools for white children, implying a segregated system where financial burdens for one racial group's schools would not fall on another. Therefore, it is classified as Jim Crow. The confidence is high due to the explicit racial language. The document type is 'codes' as it is presented as part of a compiled statute (Kentucky Statutes 1909).

classification.summary: This statute outlines the establishment and administration of graded common school districts in Kentucky. It details requirements for district boundaries, schoolhouse locations, and the process for changing district boundaries. Notably, it includes a provision (14) explicitly stating that taxes collected for white schools must be from white persons' property and taxes for colored schools must be from colored persons' property, making any apportionment between them void. This demonstrates a clear mandate for racial segregation in the funding and operation of schools.
classification.reasoning: The statute explicitly mandates racial segregation in school funding by stating that 'The property of white persons must be taxed for white schools and that of colored persons for colored schools.' This is a clear indicator of Jim Crow legislation. The confidence is high due to the explicit mention of 'white and colored schools' and the directive for separate taxation based on race. The category is 'education' as the statute pertains to school districts and their operations. classification.title: Colored graded schools - establishment of
classification.summary: This statute explicitly mandates the segregation of schools based on race. It states that provisions for graded common school districts apply to districts organized by colored people, with the word 'colored' to be substituted for 'white' where applicable. Crucially, it prohibits white individuals from voting in colored school elections, prevents the taxation of white property for colored schools, and vice versa. It also forbids white children from attending colored schools and colored children from attending white schools.
classification.reasoning: The statute explicitly mentions 'colored graded schools' and 'white districtsherein provided for', and then proceeds to outline separate and unequal provisions for each. It explicitly states that 'No white person shall vote at any election held by the colored people... nor shall the property of any white person be taxed to maintain any graded common school for colored children; nor shall the property of any colored person be taxed for the benefit of any graded common school for white children, nor shall any white child attend any graded common school for colored children... nor shall any colored child attend any graded common school for white children.' This is a clear example of a Jim Crow law mandating racial segregation in education.

classification.title: Separate Schools for White and Colored.
classification.summary: This statute mandates the separation of white and colored individuals in educational institutions. It prohibits teaching both races in the same college, school, or institution, with penalties for violations. It also makes it unlawful for individuals of one race to attend schools where the other race is received as pupils, with fines for each day of attendance. Exceptions are made for penal institutions and houses of reform. The law also allows for separate and distinct branches of private institutions in different localities, at least twenty-five miles apart, for the exclusive education of one race.
classification.reasoning: The statute explicitly mandates separate educational facilities for white and colored individuals, which is a hallmark of Jim Crow laws. It outlines penalties for operating integrated schools and for individuals attending schools with the opposite race. The mention of 'white and colored' and 'negro' clearly indicates a racial basis for the law. The document appears to be part of a compiled code of statutes from 1909, hence 'codes' is the appropriate document type. The category is 'education' as the statute directly addresses schools and colleges.

classification.title: Sinking Fund - Trustees for Agricultural and Mechanical College and State Normal School for Colored Persons
classification.summary: This statute details the allocation of interest from a perpetual bond of the Commonwealth of Kentucky to two educational institutions: the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Kentucky and the State Normal School for Colored Persons of Kentucky. The total annual interest of $4,950 is divided, with $627.75 allocated to the State Normal School for Colored Persons and $4,322.25 to the Agricultural and Mechanical College. This section is derived from an act of May 21, 1897, which also included initial appropriations to these institutions.
keywords: state normal school for colored persons
classification.reasoning: The statute explicitly names the 'State Normal School for Colored Persons of Kentucky,' indicating a racially segregated educational system. The allocation of funds, while seemingly equitable in proportion to the total bond, is a direct consequence of and perpetuates racial segregation in education. Therefore, it is classified as a Jim Crow law. The confidence is high because of the explicit mention of race. The document type is 'codes' as it is presented as a section within the Kentucky Statutes of 1909, which is a compilation of laws.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the process for local elections to determine whether to prohibit the running at large of cattle, or specific species of cattle, within a county or district. It details petition requirements, notice procedures, ballot wording, penalties for violations, owner liability for damages, and the impounding of livestock. The results of such elections are to be declared and recorded similarly to county officer elections, with provisions for contests.
classification.reasoning: The statute concerns regulations for livestock, specifically cattle, and the process for local communities to vote on whether to allow them to run at large. There is no mention of race, nor any indication of differential treatment based on race. The enforcement mechanisms and penalties apply universally to any individual who violates the elected regulations regarding livestock. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

§ 4874-91 [Ch . 136 .WORK -HOUSES .
§ 4874. Fine may be paid or replevied credit for time. When any one is com-
mitted to pay a fine he may , at any time , pay or replevy the balance due
on the judgment , and he shall thereupon be discharged ; and if one is
committed to pay a fine , and also to serve a term in lieu of imprison-
ment in jail , he may , at any time , have the days he has served placed as a
credit on the time he is committed to serve in lieu of such imprisonment ,
and when he shall serve out such term , and shall pay or replevy the bal-
ance of the judgment , he shall be thereupon discharged . (See , further ,
secs . 1377-1382 .)
§ 4875. Escaped prisoner- penalty. Any prisoner who shall escape from
the work -house or from the custody of any one to whom he may be com-
mitted , shall , on conviction thereof before the judge of the county court
or a justice of the peace of that county in which the work -house is sit-
uated , be fined ten times the amount due on the judgment under which he
was committed ; and if said fine for the escape is paid or replevied , the
prisoner shall thereupon be discharged from custody , and from all lia-
bility on the former judgment ; but if it is not paid or replevied , he shall
be committed to the work -house to pay by work the amount of the fine , at
the rate of one dollar for each day's work actually done .
§ 4876. County court and city council may own jointly. The county court of
any county and the council or board of trustees of any city or town in it
may contract for the joint use for the purposes of this act , whether such
house shall be owned by the county or by the town or city , or by both .
§ 4877. County court- who constitute. The term county court , as used in
this act , means a court in which shall be present a majority of the justices
of the peace of the county .
§ 4878. Courts of two counties may own jointly The county courts of any
two or more counties are authorized to contract for the joint construc-
tion , management , and use of a work -house for such counties .
§ 4879. Submission of question to voters. No appropriation for the erec
tion of a work -house under the provisions of this act shall be made by a
county court until the question of making the appropriation shall be sub-
mitted , at a regular election , to the voters of the county , and a majority
of those voting shall vote in favor of said appropriation .
